name: aHash
baseline: xxHash (XXH3 via xxhash-rust) and wyhash; also SipHash-1-3, the Rust std HashMap default
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks that hash a u64 and strings of 1-1023 bytes through Rust's Hasher/BuildHasher trait (compare/tests/compare.rs), compared with SipHash, FxHash, FnvHash, FarmHash, HighwayHash, MetroHash, t1ha, xxh3 and wyhash. The "50GB/s" figure comes from the SMHasher bulk test (smhasher/ahashOutput.txt: 60349 MiB/s average at a nominal "3 ghz")
claimed_speedup: Page text (verbatim): "AHash is faster than either one [t1ha and XXHash], both with and without AES"; "AHash outperforms wyHash across all input sizes"; "At over 50GB/s aHash is the fastest algorithm to pass the full test suite by more than a factor of 2"; about 10x faster than SipHash. The Google Sheet linked from the page gives time to hash a u64 and a 1 KB string (units not labelled, probably ns): AHash 0.87 / 19.98, XXHash (xxh3) 11.88 / 114.14, WyHash 1.53 / 53.13, SipHash-1-3 9.70 / 219.13, FxHash 0.71 / 121.97. That makes aHash about 13.7x / 5.7x faster than xxh3, 1.76x / 2.66x faster than wyhash, and 11x / 11x faster than SipHash-1-3 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc (version unstated); bench profile in compare/Cargo.toml: opt-level=3, lto='fat', codegen-units=1, debug-assertions=false; Criterion 0.3.3; target-cpu/RUSTFLAGS unstated
stars_or_usage: 1347 GitHub stars; about 790M crates.io downloads (about 151M recent) and 2051 reverse dependencies. It was hashbrown's default hasher until hashbrown v0.15.0 (2024-10), which switched to foldhash. It was never the Rust std HashMap default, which is SipHash-1-3.
tradeoffs: Output is not fixed/standardized across hardware and versions, so unsuitable for persisted or transmitted hashes; DOS-resistance relies on per-process random keys.
caveats: No CPU model or rustc version is stated, and the sheet does not label its time units. Comparisons go through Rust Hasher-trait wrappers, which may penalise streaming hashes such as xxh3 on 1 KB inputs. The independent rurban/SMHasher table (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) contradicts the bulk-speed claims: ahash64 9862.62 MiB/s against xxh3 20853.74 and wyhash 22640.53. It shows aHash only slightly ahead on small keys (27.32 cycles/hash against 29.46 for xxh3 and 28.91 for wyhash). The "fastest SMHasher-passing algorithm by >2x" claim is stale. Output is not stable across platforms or versions (HashMap use only). FxHash is faster on u64 keys, as the page admits.
found_via: gh search repos "non-cryptographic hash" --sort stars; compare/readme.md opened directly

verification.tier_reason: First-party benchmark only: the Criterion bench code is public (compare/tests/compare.rs, with the bench profile in compare/Cargo.toml) and the linked Google Sheet gives per-hasher timings, but no CPU model and no rustc version are stated. The one independent suite, rurban/SMHasher, does not back the win: it shows aHash losing about 2x on bulk throughput to xxh3 and wyhash and winning only slightly on small keys, so this cannot be B.
verification.notes: The quotes in the record match the page word for word. The record understated the evidence: the linked sheet does have tabular numbers. Fixed the license (the repo is dual MIT/Apache-2.0, not just Apache-2.0) and the usage claim, since aHash was hashbrown's default hasher until v0.15 and was never the std default. Independent SMHasher data contradicts the bulk-throughput superiority claim, so tier stays C with a strong caveat.

name: VecFalcon (Vectorized Falcon-Sign)
baseline: C-FN-DSA (Thomas Pornin's FN-DSA/Falcon implementation, github.com/pornin/c-fn-dsa at commit 96e3b92), SHAKE256X4 variant
workload: Falcon-512/1024 sign_core (SHAKE256X4 PRNG variant; SHAKE256X8 on AVX-512F) CPU-cycle medians over 10,000 runs (x86, ARM) or 2,000 runs (RISC-V) across SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512F, NEON, RV64GC, RV64GCB, RV64GCV and RV64GCVB. Also micro-benchmarks of the vectorized BaseSampler and the RVV/RV64D FFT/iFFT.
claimed_speedup: Falcon-512 sign_core cycles vs the C-FN-DSA reference: 1.13x SSE2, 1.23x AVX2, 1.36x AVX-512F, 1.17x NEON, 1.37x RV64GC, 1.36x RV64GCB, 1.58x RV64GCV, 1.59x RV64GCVB (the paper reports these as 13-59% improvements). Falcon-1024: 1.14x-1.59x. The BaseSampler core without PRNG is 4.2x (SSE2), 8.4x (AVX2), 9.8x (AVX-512F), 7.7x (RVV), 3.8x (RV64IM) and 1.8x (NEON) faster than the C-FN-DSA ref core. With PRNG included it is 1.3x-2.7x. RVV FFT/iFFT is 4.1x-4.7x faster than ref on the SpacemiT X60, and RV64D FFT/iFFT is 2.7x-3.0x faster.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04); Clang 10.0.0 (ARM, Ubuntu 20.04); GCC 13.2.0 (RISC-V, Bianbu 1.0.15). All builds use -O2 -DFNDSA_SHAKE256X4=1. x86 builds pin the ISA with -msse2, -mavx2 or -mavx512f plus -mno-* flags for higher extensions. RISC-V builds use -march=rv64gc, rv64gc_zba_zbb, rv64gcv or rv64gcv_zba_zbb.
hardware: Intel i7-11700K (Rocket Lake, 3.6GHz, Turbo Boost and Hyper-Threading disabled); ARM Cortex-A72 (Raspberry Pi 4B, 1.5GHz); SpacemiT X60, RVV v1.0 VLEN=256 (Milk-V Jupiter, 2.0GHz)
license: MIT (root LICENSE). The C-FN-DSA-derived opt/ and ref/ directories carry the Unlicense. opt/fft_neon.c is Apache-2.0 (derived from GMUCERG Falcon_NEON).
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; IACR TCHES 2026 accepted paper artifact
tradeoffs: Baseline is the C-FN-DSA reference implementation, not liboqs's own bundled Falcon backend directly, though the two are architecturally related (liboqs's Falcon derives from the same lineage of reference/optimized code); the vectorized BaseSampler deliberately breaks bit-for-bit KAT reproducibility with official test vectors while preserving verification interoperability
caveats: Gains are for signature generation (sign_core) only, not keygen or verify, and are measured on the SHAKE256X4 variant, which is not KAT-compatible with default Falcon signing (interoperable for verification). Part of the gain comes from integrated third-party code: XKCP 8-way Keccak on AVX-512F; the BK22 hybrid Keccak and NG23 NEON FFT on ARM; ZYHK25 Keccak on RISC-V. The paper measured C-FN-DSA as faster than the NIST-submission AVX2 code on the i7-11700K, so it is a strong baseline. The only direct comparison with other optimized prior work is at the BaseSampler level (NG23 NEON is slower than ref). Licensing is mixed: MIT, Unlicense (public-domain dedication, no patent grant) and Apache-2.0 files. GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION.
found_via: GitHub graphql search: 'falcon signature avx2 in:name,description,readme'

verification.tier_reason: The ePrint 2025/1867 paper (published in TCHES 2026, DOI 10.46586/tches.v2026.i1.302-324) benchmarks sign_core against the C-FN-DSA reference at commit 96e3b92 (Table 6) and states the compiler (GCC 13.3.0, Clang 10.0.0, GCC 13.2.0), the flags (-O2, -DFNDSA_SHAKE256X4=1, per-ISA -m/-march flags) and the CPUs (i7-11700K, Cortex-A72, SpacemiT X60). The artifact repo ships the benchmark code for both sides (opt/speed_fndsa.c and ref/speed_fndsa.c with per-platform Makefiles, plus profiling/ for BaseSampler and FFT) and the raw outputs (opt/ and ref/speed_fndsa_*.txt), which match Table 6.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers check out against Tables 4-6 of the paper and the repo's raw speed files. The one overstatement was 'up to 8.4x faster than prior work': 8.4x is the AVX2 BaseSampler core vs the C-FN-DSA ref, and the maximum is 9.8x on AVX-512F. The record's metric is 'throughput', but the paper measures per-signature cycle latency. Metadata verified: 4 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2025-12-05 (active), usability copyable (all components are under OSI licenses).
